ety.text: * From Middle English cause (also with the sense of “a thing”), borrowed from Old French cause (“a cause, a thing”), borrowed from Latin causa (“reason, sake, cause”), from Proto-Italic *kaussā, which is of unknown origin. Doublet of chose (“(law) a thing; personal property”). See accuse, excuse, recuse, ruse. Displaced native Old English intinga. * From Middle English causen, Old French causer and Medieval Latin causāre.

senses.d: The source of, or reason for, an event or action; that which produces or effects a result.
ex: They identified a burst pipe as the cause of the flooding.

We thanke you both, yet one but flatters vs,
As well appeareth by the cauſe you come,
Namely, to appeale each other of high treaſon.

senses.d: Sufficient reason.
ex: There is no cause for alarm.
The end of the war was a cause for celebration.

senses.d: A goal, aim or principle, especially one which transcends purely selfish ends.
ex: God befriend us, as our cause is just.
The part they take against me is from zeal to the cause.

senses.d: Sake; interest; advantage.
ex: I did it not for his cause.

senses.d: Any subject of discussion or debate; a matter; an affair.
ex: What counsel give you in this weighty cause?

senses.d: A suit or action in court; any legal process by which a party endeavors to obtain his claim, or what he regards as his right; case; ground of action.
To set off an event or action; to bring about; to produce.
ex: The lightning caused thunder.

senses.d: To actively produce as a result, by means of force or authority.
ex: His dogged determination caused the fundraising to be successful.
I will cause it to rain upon the earth forty days.

senses.d: To assign or show cause; to give a reason; to make excuse.
ex: He, to shifte their curious request, / Gan causen why she could not come in place.

grp.label: source or reason of an event or action
to set off an event or action

senses.d: A usually preliminary meeting of party members to nominate candidates for public office or delegates to be sent to a nominating convention, or to confer regarding policy.
A grouping of all the members of a legislature from the same party.
A political interest group by members of a legislative body.
To meet and participate in a caucus.
ex: The diehard Republicans of Kansas caucused today and delivered a big victory for Mike Huckabee, McCain's remaining serious challenger.

senses.d: To confer.
ex: The protesters caucused nearby to discuss demands.

senses.d: To bring into or treat in a caucus.

ety.text: Recorded since 1297 as Middle English caucioun (“bail, guarantee, pledge”), from Old French caution (“security, surety”), itself from Latin cautiō, from cautus, past participle of caveō, cavēre (“be on one's guard”).

senses.d: Prudence when faced with, or when expecting to face, danger; care taken in order to avoid risk or harm.
ex: take caution
have caution

senses.d: A careful attention to the probable effects of an act, in order that failure or harm may be avoided.
ex: The guideline expressed caution against excessive radiographic imaging.

senses.d: Security; guaranty; bail.
ex: The Parliament would yet give his majesty sufficient caution that the war should be vigorously prosecuted.

senses.d: One who draws attention or causes astonishment by their behaviour.
ex: Oh, that boy, he's a caution! He does make me laugh.
‘You are a caution,’ she said, when she came out. ‘I don't understand you.’

senses.d: A formal warning given as an alternative to prosecution in minor cases.
A yellow card.
To warn; to alert, advise that caution is warranted.
ex: "Careful, Uwe," cautions my Venezuelan explorer friend, José Miguel Pérez, with a grim smile. "You're too big for us to carry back down."

senses.d: To read someone their formal legal rights as part of a lawful arrest.
ex: They're under arrest. Caution them, will you?

senses.d: To give a yellow card.

grp.label: precept or warning against evil or danger
